title: Koala — Linux VMs for your Mac
excerpt: Run Linux workloads on your Mac, each in its own lightweight virtual machine.
content_html:
Preview · 0.1.0-preview.11 · Apple silicon · macOS 26+

Linux workloads on your Mac, one VM each.

Koala runs jobs, services, development environments and AI agents in ARM64 Linux VMs on Apple silicon. Each VM has its own kernel, disk and network, and gets only the access you grant it.

$brew install kunalkushwaha/koala/koala

Watch

Koala, run agents with confidence

Section titled “Koala, run agents with confidence”

The explainer is also on YouTube.

01 · Install

Two commands, no sudo

Section titled “Two commands, no sudo”

You need a Mac with Apple silicon and macOS 26 or newer, and images built for linux/arm64. To install from a release archive, see getting started.

02 · Try it

From throwaway job to sandboxed agent

Section titled “From throwaway job to sandboxed agent”

  • Throwaway job
  • VM that stays up
  • Sandboxed agent
  • Agent from a template

A command in a fresh VM that is removed when the command ends:

03 · What you get

Built for untrusted workloads

Section titled “Built for untrusted workloads”

Throwaway jobs

A command in a fresh VM, removed when it ends. For builds, tests and scripts you would rather not run on your Mac. Jobs and VMs →

Services and environments

VMs that keep running after your terminal closes. exec, attach a shell, cp files in and out. Working inside a VM →

Keys stay on your Mac

An agent’s API keys stay in your login keychain. The broker adds a key only to the requests a policy allows, so it never enters the VM. Keys on your Mac →

Agents in one command

koala create hermes --template hermes makes an agent’s VM, its key’s policy, a volume and its setup, after showing the plan. VM templates →

The images you have

OCI images from Docker Hub or a private registry, pinned by digest when a VM is created. Images →

Lean or full

Lean runs one image with a minimal init. Full runs Ubuntu 24.04 with systemd and Docker Engine. Profiles →

Deny by default

No host files, no secrets, no LAN, no other VMs, until you grant them. Checked on the Mac side. Networking →

Runs as you

A per-user launchd manager keeps track of your VMs. Nothing system-wide, no root daemon. Getting started →

04 · Defaults

What a VM can reach

Section titled “What a VM can reach”

Resource Default When you grant it
Internet Public addresses only Can be switched off
Files on your Mac None Folders you share; read-only unless you ask for read-write
Secrets None Named secrets, to one VM, as a file or an environment variable
API keys None A broker grant: the key stays on your Mac, added only to the requests a policy allows
Services on your Mac None One address and specific ports
Your LAN None A specific prefix and ports
Other VMs Never Not available in v0.1
Published ports None On 127.0.0.1, or on the LAN when you ask

Koala treats everything inside a VM as untrusted, and trusts you, the logged-in macOS user. VMs do not keep running after you log out or restart your Mac.
